abstract: Legislatures influence executive agencies through oversight. We argue that individual legislators’ preferences—in addition to institution-level preferences—can influence agencies’ actions, especially when legislators are in the majority party. Using data on 216,331 inspections of 17,913 nursing homes conducted by US state agencies between 2000 and 2017, we test the independent and conditional influence of both individual legislators and collective legislative institutions on the number of citations that agencies issue to nursing homes. We show that agencies issue 6 percent more citations per inspection to nursing homes in districts with liberal legislators and 20 percent more citations in states with liberal legislatures. We also demonstrate that individual legislators’ influence is conditional on majority party status, at least in states’ upper chambers, with nursing homes in a liberal member’s district experiencing more citations when the legislator is in the majority party. Overall, our findings show that both individual members and collective institutions influence agencies, but the influence of the former is partially contingent on the latter.
title: Oversight from below and above: individual and institutional legislative influence on agencies

abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our theoretical results with a series of experiments involving generative text and image models. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist under strong competition. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02761 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI

abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors acknowledge funding from the University of Konstanz for Study 2, Harvard University Pershing Square Foundation for Human Research, and Harvard Business School. The funders had no role in data collection and analysis, the decision to publish, or preparation of this manuscript. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03600 .
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences (INFORMS)
title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through

abstract: This study investigates the impact of fine-grained flood exposure on housing market prices when mandatory flood insurance and lender-required flood zone disclosure are absent. Existing literature documents flood-related price discounts, yet most rely on binary measures and evidence from North America and Europe. Using 12,464 residential transactions in Macao from 2006 to 2024, we estimate hedonic models with building and subdistrict-by-year fixed effects utilizing high-resolution graduated hazard maps. Following major typhoons and the public release of hazard maps, our findings indicate 8–14% lower property values across hazard levels that binary measures miss, suggestive of risk perception when flood information becomes salient. Heterogeneity across flood hazard levels is consistent with the combined differences in coastal amenity value and flood protection. The results provide market-based evidence that can inform flood insurance and flood-defense investment even without mandatory flood zone disclosure.
title: How Flood Risk Shapes Property Prices in a Dense Coastal City: Evidence from Graduated Hazard Maps in Macao

abstract: I provide insights into income changes measured in surveys using single questions, by extending to longitudinal settings a measurement error model previously developed in the literature. In this framework, single-question income data are validated against a benchmark provided by detailed source-by-source questions, which are considered the best practice for measuring income in surveys. I outline the assumptions required to infer benchmark income changes between two time periods (e.g., two subsequent survey waves), both at the macro- and micro-levels, when income is collected using single questions. Recovering meaningful income changes from such measures requires assuming that respondents’ misreporting behaviour is time-invariant. The use of single-question income changes as dependent and independent variables in linear models, and potential heterogeneity in respondents’ misreporting behaviour are also discussed. I apply the methodology to estimate income changes in Italy between 2022 and 2023, using data from a new web-survey conducted by the Bank of Italy.
title: Income changes and measurement error in single-question measures of household income*

abstract: Contracts that settle on a market price invite trading that moves the price at settlement, and the standard remedy is a time-weighted average price. Whether the average removes the incentive is rarely observed. Polymarket’s five-minute bitcoin contract paid on a single Chainlink price snapshot until 7 August 2026 and on a 30-second and then a 60-second average afterwards. We measure the settlement footprint in Binance spot data at 82,752 five-minute boundaries. Under snapshot settlement the final-ten-second volume share rose from 3.05 to 5.68 percent, tenfold volume spikes became six times as frequent, and near-the-strike prices reverted. The footprint vanished in the week of the switch. In the first three weeks of the 60-second average the share was within 0.03 percentage points of its pre-launch level, volume did not migrate to earlier bins, and near-the-strike moves no longer reverted. Liquidity rewards that Polymarket paid market makers for quoting the contract after the switch came to less than 0.2 percent of its turnover, and the footprint did not return when they were briefly withdrawn in mid-August.
title: Does a time-weighted average price deter settlement manipulation? Evidence from Polymarket’s five-minute bitcoin markets

abstract: Once a good idea comes to mind, it is hard to avoid wondering why no one else has already taken advantage of it. Is it because the idea is not as good as it initially appears? This concern gives rise to a dilemma over whether to pursue the idea or abandon it despite its apparent promise, a dilemma we call “the good idea dilemma”. Paradoxically, the more compelling an idea appears, the more puzzling it becomes that others have not exploited it, thereby deepening the dilemma. We study this dilemma in a continuous-time game with multiple players, analyzing idea adoption dynamics and their economic implications. The dilemma yields both under-implementation of good ideas and over-implementation of bad ideas. Its adverse consequences equally affect trivial ideas that arise frequently and creative ideas that rarely do, but intensify for ideas accessible to larger audiences or with riskier outcomes, even under risk neutrality.
title: The Good Idea Dilemma

abstract: Urban streets provide spatial contexts in which pedestrian activity unfolds over time, yet previous research has seldom examined how these street rhythms differ across space or how they are associated with local street conditions. This study addresses this gap by examining street-level pedestrian rhythms across Seoul’s commercial streets. Using mobile phone signal–based estimates of pedestrian presence for 110,574 street segments in 2022, we extract 11 temporal features from weekday pedestrian time series and apply fuzzy C-means clustering to identify five street rhythm types. Multinomial logistic regression evaluates how these rhythms relate to 16 indicators of commercial hierarchy, physical scale, accessibility, functional mix, and surrounding populations. The findings show that street rhythm types are systematically associated with multiple dimensions of spatial context, rather than reflecting simple differences in pedestrian-presence levels or land-use intensity. Even among commercially active streets, evening-peak rhythms were distinguished by concentrations of retail, leisure, and entertainment-oriented functions. Midday- and afternoon-peak rhythms, despite their similar daytime profiles, were also differentiated by their spatial contexts: midday-peak rhythms were associated with office- and institution-based workday districts, whereas afternoon-peak rhythms were linked to production-related commercial areas. By revealing these distinctions, this underscores the value of treating time as an integral dimension of urban spatial structure.
title: Shaping street rhythms: Spatial context and the temporal patterns of pedestrian activity

abstract: We match French export and Madagascan import declarations using container identifiers and account for shipment-specific transport costs to identify declarations and firms at risk of tariff evasion, examine how evasion occurs, and assess customs enforcement. Tariff liabilities calculated from French declarations exceed those based on corresponding Madagascan declarations by 24 percent in aggregate. This tariff revenue gap is highly concentrated: the five importers with the largest positive gaps account for three-quarters of it. Undervaluation accounts for approximately two-thirds of implied tariff revenue losses, with product misclassification accounting for the remainder. Larger-value containers facing high tariffs appear at greater risk of evasion. Many reporting discrepancies are nevertheless inconsistent with tariff minimization: For approximately two-fifths of containers, tariff liabilities calculated from Madagascan declarations exceed those based on French declarations. Customs value adjustments are ineffective, reducing implied tariff revenue losses by only 1.8 percent.
title: Detecting tariff evasion: Evidence from matched container data

abstract: We study an AK-type growth model in which production relies on fertile land, an irreplaceable factor that is physically bounded. Unlike the standard AK framework, productive capacity cannot expand without limit because production generates pollution that degrades fertile land, while abatement can restore it. Using Pontryagin’s state-constrained optimal control approach, we transform physical state constraints into control constraints and obtain a complete analytical characterization of the optimal solution. The analysis identifies three regimes determined by the discount rate. For sufficiently patient planners, fertile land reaches its maximum feasible level in finite time and consumption converges to its highest sustainable level. For intermediate discount rates, land and consumption decline gradually, while very impatient planners choose no abatement and rapidly deplete productive capacity. The results highlight how physical limits reshape optimal growth and resource-management policies and provide new insights for environmental and resource economics.
title: AK growth with a bounded productive factor

abstract: This paper studies how an unemployment-benefit reform in one member state of a monetary union affects savings, net foreign asset positions, and fiscal space across member states when households face incomplete insurance. Lower benefits reduce unemployment and increase fiscal space in the reforming country. Employed workers increase their precautionary savings to compensate for reduced public insurance. A portion of these savings is invested abroad, pushing the non-reforming country into a negative net foreign asset position and lowering its long-run consumption. Despite raising fiscal space and long-run average consumption in the reforming country, the reform may decrease ex-ante welfare because it reduces insurance and depresses consumption during the transition as households self-insure through higher savings. We discipline our proposed model with firm-level evidence on Germany’s post-reform tradable-sector expansion following the Hartz IV reform of unemployment benefits. In our simulation, this reform accounts for a substantial share of the observed post-reform open-economy adjustment, whereas the earlier wage moderation cannot explain most of the observed patterns.
title: Incomplete insurance and open-economy spillovers of labor market reforms

abstract: We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread. To our knowledge, this is the first transaction-level evidence on price formation in these markets. A $1 billion long-USD order flow depreciates the domestic spot rate by about 10 basis points and the offshore NDF rate by about 18 basis points. The spot impact is larger when dealer balance sheets are tight. Policy episodes in the Chinese renminbi, Malaysian ringgit, and Indian rupee show how changes in offshore speculative activity and arbitrage between offshore and onshore markets affect the spread and domestic exchange rates. We rationalize these findings with a model in which offshore demand pressure generates NDF order flow, dealers hedge inventory through domestic spot markets, and capital controls limit intermediation between offshore and onshore forward markets.

abstract: Increased vertical integration and coordination are defining features of transforming and modernising agricultural value chains in low‐ and middle‐income countries, with important implications for market efficiency and farm‐level transformation. However, research documenting these processes in transforming domestic value chains is limited, with existing studies largely focusing on large firms, foreign direct investment and high‐value food products, leaving less understood how domestic processors in staple food value chains expand into complementary businesses and services. We study these processes in the rice value chain—the most important staple in Southeast Asia—in Myanmar, using unique large‐scale data from domestic rice mills and farmers. We show that both modern and traditional mills serve as key nodes in local rice value chains, fulfilling diverse roles beyond processing at both the farm and post‐harvest levels. Yet, statistical tests that control for mill and farmer characteristics, respectively, show that modern mills are more engaged in vertical integration and coordination, particularly in post‐harvest value chain segments, highlighting the co‐development of modern processing and business expansion. Consistent with this pattern in the miller data, farmers using a modern mill are more likely to receive complementary services—especially post‐harvest—and to adopt modern production practices more broadly. However, this expansion is uneven, with services reaching large farms more frequently than small and medium farms.
title: Vertical Integration and Coordination in Modernising Staple Food Value Chains: Evidence From Myanmar's Rice Sector

abstract: The 2026 US–Iran war disrupted global energy markets, particularly in economies dependent on imported fossil fuels. Pakistan, given its geographic proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and high reliance on imported oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), was expected to face severe stress in its electricity sector. However, a comparison of key energy-sector indicators before and during the conflict, benchmarked against the 2022 Russia–Ukraine energy-price shock, suggests that the impact on Pakistan’s electricity sector was comparatively moderate relative to the 2022 energy-price shock, despite the severity of the external shock. The evidence indicates that the rapid expansion of distributed solar played an important role by reducing reliance on imported fuels and weakening the transmission of international fuel-price volatility into domestic electricity markets. These findings reveal that distributed renewable energy can serve not only as a pathway to decarbonization but also as a strategic instrument for strengthening energy security and resilience to geopolitical shocks in an increasingly volatile global energy landscape.
title: Solar PV as a buffer against energy security risks during geopolitical shocks: The case of Pakistan during the 2026 US–Iran war

abstract: Mean field equilibrium (MFE) has emerged as a computationally tractable solution concept for large dynamic games. However, computing MFE remains challenging due to nonlinearities and the absence of contraction properties, limiting its reliability for counterfactual analysis and comparative statics. This paper studies dynamic models in which agents interact through a small number of functions of the population distribution, with particular emphasis on the scalar case. Such low-dimensional interactions naturally arise in a wide range of applications in economics and operations. The main contribution of this paper is to introduce iterative algorithms that leverage this structure and have provide global convergence guarantees for computing and learning MFE under mild assumptions. Unlike existing approaches, our algorithms do not require monotonicity or contraction properties. We also provide model-free algorithms that learn an approximate MFE from simulation using reinforcement learning methods, without requiring prior knowledge of payoff or transition functions. Beyond computation, we establish existence of stationary MFE for non-compact state spaces. For scalar interactions, we also derive analytical comparative statics without requiring monotonicity of the equilibrium mapping. We apply our methods to classical models of dynamic competition, including capacity competition; to heterogeneous-agent macroeconomic models; and to models motivated by online marketplaces and learning, including inventory competition, ridesharing, and social learning. The applications illustrate how changes in market parameters affect equilibrium outcomes and how the algorithms can be used for reliable counterfactual analysis.
journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

abstract: While existing evidence shows that increased school spending improves student outcomes, it remains unclear whether current spending levels are efficient. Building on the classic public finance insight that local public-goods provision is efficient when a marginal, tax-financed increase leaves local house prices unchanged, we test whether school spending meets this benchmark. To implement this test, we assemble a 26-year national panel linking house prices, current public school expenditures, and property taxes, and exploit court-mandated school finance reforms to develop new instruments for local taxation. Combining these instruments with established instruments for current expenditures, we estimate the causal effect of tax-financed spending increases on house prices. Tax-financed increases in current expenditures raise house prices, implying that households value additional school spending more than it costs. These findings indicate that current U.S. public school spending falls below the efficient benchmark.
title: Does the United States spend enough on public schools? Evidence from a market-based efficiency test

abstract: How do firms adjust their labor demand when a female employee takes temporary leave after childbirth? Using Austrian administrative data, we compare firms with and without a birth event and exploit policy reforms that significantly altered leave durations. We find three main results. First, firms respond primarily through anticipatory hiring, while medium-run effects on total employment and the wage bill are small. Second, these adjustments differ sharply by gender: anticipatory replacement hiring is overwhelmingly female, but firms’ workforce composition shifts toward men in the medium run, driven by the shorter tenure of female new hires and higher retention of male incumbents. Third, while longer leave entitlements substantially extend actual leave absences, we do not find systematic differences in firms’ labor demand responses across leave regimes. Taken together, these findings show that firms accommodate parental leave mainly through anticipatory hiring and gendered changes in workforce composition, with limited medium-run changes in aggregate labor demand even when leave durations differ substantially.
title: How do firms respond to parental leave absences?

abstract: We study the welfare effects of removing explicit and implicit fossil fuel subsidies, the latter via corrective pricing of local air pollution. We map a multi-region general-equilibrium model with global supply chains to granular data on subsidies, marginal external costs, and national income and product accounts. On average, unilateral subsidy removal raises a country’s welfare by 3.2%, generates revenues equal to 3.1% of consumption, and lowers the carbon price needed for Paris targets by 46%. Non-market gains exceed market losses in most countries. Local air pollution pricing drives 97% of net benefits; removing explicit subsidies alone has minor effects on welfare and emissions. A quarter of countries would already reach their Paris climate target, making additional carbon pricing redundant. Combining subsidy removal with carbon pricing dominates carbon pricing alone everywhere. Global multilateral subsidy removal cuts emissions by 27.4% and raises global welfare, excluding climate benefits, by 2.3%. Corrective fossil fuel taxation can align economic, fiscal, and climate goals. (JEL C68, H23, Q43, Q58)
title: The welfare effects of explicit and implicit subsidies on fossil fuels

abstract: This paper examines how monetary policy affects labor income inequality and whether these effects depend on overall economic conditions. Using monthly U.S. data, we show that standard linear models find little evidence of a relationship between monetary policy and inequality. Once we allow policy effects to vary with economic conditions, however, a clear pattern emerges. During normal periods, contractionary monetary policy temporarily reduces labor income inequality. During crises, the same policy shock produces a large and persistent increase in inequality. These opposing responses help explain why standard linear estimates find little overall effect. The joint state-dependent responses of labor market tightness and inequality are consistent with an important labor-market channel in the transmission of monetary policy. More broadly, the findings suggest that monetary tightening during periods of economic stress can carry particularly adverse consequences for labor income inequality.
title: Does Monetary Policy Affect Labor Income Inequality? Evidence from State-Dependent Transmission

abstract: This paper quantifies the effects of college expansion under purely merit-based, competitive admissions, endogenizing pre-labor-market conditions. We develop a heterogeneous-agent life-cycle model where parents invest in their children’s pre-college human capital at multiple stages to compete for limited college slots. Applying the framework to China—where admissions rely solely on score ranks and enrollment has grown tenfold over the past 25 years—we find that score-based admissions increase the importance of human capital at the college admission stage relative to initial endowments. Family resources therefore shape admission indirectly through parental investment in pre-college human capital. Expanding college access under this system reduces intergenerational mobility because higher-income families respond by disproportionately increasing pre-college investments, strengthening the link between child achievement and parental income. Counterfactuals show that mobility would improve with college expansion if endogenous parental investment responses were shut down.

abstract: We investigate how school closures affect educational outcomes through parental responses. Using quasi‐experimental variation in school‐level closure days and linked administrative‐survey data, we find that 10 additional closure days raise private tutoring expenditure by 4.1% and within‐school test‐score dispersion by 25%; over the average 53‐day closure, low‐income students lose 0.09 SD. To quantify substitution between schooling and parental investment and evaluate compensatory policy, we estimate a tournament model in which schooling and tutoring jointly produce test scores. Tutoring substitutes for in‐person days, burdening low‐income households disproportionately. Counterfactuals show a means‐tested voucher fully offsets the resulting rise in inequality.
title: Mitigating School Closures: Parental Responses and Tutoring Vouchers

abstract: In a green transition, workers will have to move from polluting, carbon-intensive sectors to other sectors and firms. To shed light on adjustment costs for workers in the green transition, this column uses German administrative data to estimate the cost of involuntary job displacement for workers in high-carbon-intensity sectors. Such workers face larger earnings and wage losses than workers displaced in other sectors. Production processes in carbon-intensive sectors are also regionally concentrated and involve specific occupations and tasks with higher firm-wage premia, reducing worker options for finding jobs with similar skill requirements and pay.
authors: César Barreto, Robert Grundke, Ze’ev Krill
title: The cost of job loss in carbon-intensive sectors: Evidence from Germany

abstract: Mortality is one of the most salient consequences of climate change. Existing estimates have largely focused on the direct effects of local heat exposure. This column argues that this perspective can miss an important part of the overall health burden. New evidence based on fluctuations in global temperature suggests that climate change also affects mortality indirectly through its effects on economic activity and living standards. Accounting for these broader channels substantially increases estimated mortality damages and highlights an important role for economic resilience in limiting the health consequences of climate change.
authors: Adrien Bilal, Diego Känzig, Krzysztof Lisiecki
title: The mortality costs of climate change

abstract: In the presence of gender-specific barriers, certain workplace environments and amenities may be particularly important for women, yet difficult to observe during job search due to information frictions. A large-scale field experiment on Pakistan's online job board publicized these job characteristics—namely, supervisor gender, coworker gender composition, work flexibility, commuting support, and overnight travel requirements. Information on these characteristics was randomly disclosed in job advertisements and email alerts. Analysis at the job-alert level shows that female jobseekers respond to supervisor gender, remote work, and commuting support. At the job level, when these characteristics were disclosed, the number of female applicants increased as the jobs were more favorable to women.

title: Job Characteristics That Matter for Women: Evidence from a Large-Scale Experiment in Pakistan

abstract: This paper introduces the notion of $$\mathcal {G}$$ -rules, which extend the Pareto rule when populations are endogenous. Societal evaluations of lives are required. $$\mathcal {G}$$ -rules compare pairs of allocations whenever evaluating the gains of some agents—utility gains or benefits of (not) being born—against the losses of others is not required. $$\mathcal {G}$$ -efficiency naturally arises. The $$\mathcal {A}$$ and $$\mathcal {P}$$ criteria of Golosov et al. (2007) are special cases. Transitive $$\mathcal {G}$$ -rules admit an axiomatic foundation based on normatively appealing properties and can be conveniently represented with $$\mathcal {G}$$ -nondecreasing critical levels. Many public policies that distort fertility decisions are $$\mathcal {G}$$ -efficient because they benefit children who are (not) born as a result of these policies.
title: Generalizing the Pareto principle with endogenous populations

abstract: Asymmetric trading costs arise when shipping times from point i to point j differ from shipping from point j to i. We show that such asymmetric trading costs predict distinct patterns of location in a class of models using Anderson-Dixit-Stiglitz preferences, where advantage in import market access (or potential) is more beneficial than that in export market access. We bring this prediction to the data, as well as additional ones along the lines of a number of propositions, while also controlling for local micro-geographic characteristics and using data on the location and sizes of cities in ancient Greece. Prevailing winds create an environment of asymmetric and seasonally varying trading costs in ancient Greece. We find that trade potential is strongly associated with the location and size of poleis. The model’s directional prediction is supported when trade potential is measured using the left and right eigenvector centralities implied by the model: import-oriented centrality has a larger coefficient than export-oriented centrality. The result is less robust for alternative reduced-form measures. Using 2SLS methods for population-weighted market access, we find significant differences between export and import market access, with the former often more important than the latter. These findings show that directional asymmetries in trading costs matter for urbanization, while also suggesting that their empirical implications depend on how directional access is measured.
title: Asymmetric trading costs and ancient Greek cities

abstract: In Bukavu and other Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) cities, food security faces significant challenges due to rapid population growth, war-driven immigration, and a governmental orientation towards the mineral sector. These issues are exacerbated by the exodus from farming communities, low agricultural yields, and poor infrastructure limiting access to farming inputs and local markets. Consequently, local communities rely heavily on food imports, often becoming vulnerable to accessing only highly processed, nutrient-poor foods. This study examines how these factors, combined with reduced local food production and poor infrastructure, impact food security in the city. First, a literature review was conducted to map relevant actors and existing research on food security, nutrition, and health policies. Focus group discussions were then conducted with nutritionists, urban planners, policymakers, local authorities, private sector actors, academics, and consumers, as well as key informant interviews with users and providers of both formal and informal food services, to gain a deeper understanding of these factors. Our analysis reveals that Bukavu’s history is deeply intertwined with extractivism, marked by conflict and resource exploitation, shaping its economy, infrastructure, and governance, often at the expense of local communities and the environment. This dynamic has had lasting impacts on key food security drivers and contributed to social instability. We consider implications for improving food security in Bukavu, taking into account pressures from extractivism, the demographic boom, and ongoing conflict. This study aims to better understand food security in conflict-affected regions and offers insights for policy and intervention development.
title: Food security at the crossroads of conflict and economic priorities: the case of Bukavu, DRC
